newsitem.title: GERMANY: SOCCER-EINTRACHT FRANKFURT BATTLING TO AVOID DROP INTO OBSCURITY.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-EINTRACHT FRANKFURT BATTLING TO AVOID DROP INTO OBSCURITY.

text.p: A book published last week in Britain on the 100 best soccer matches played had the most famous club match of all time at the top of the list -- the 1960 European Cup final in which Real Madrid beat Eintracht Frankfurt 7-3 in front of 134,000 at Glasgow's Hampden Park.

On any other day against any other opposition Eintracht might well have won the European Cup. But they were up against the best club side ever assembled, who chose the night of May 18, 1960, to give their greatest display.

Eintracht's part in the classic has largely been overlooked down the years, but although they were well-beaten in the end, they were not disgraced and even briefly held the lead for seven minutes midway through the first half.

But while Real have continued to live among Europe's elite, today Eintracht find themselves in very different circumstances -- battling to avoid the drop from the German second division into the semi-professional obscurity of the regional leagues.

Relegated from the Bundesliga last season, Frankfurt have had another woeful season and the club from one of Europe's richest cities is facing an impoverished future unless matters improve on and off the pitch very quickly.
Their 1959 national title, their domestic cup wins of 1974, 1975, 1981 and 1988 and their UEFA Cup success of 1980 are now long forgotten.
Frankfurt are a club in crisis with their remaining fans beleagured by the shame of relegation and scandal.
Inept performances on the pitch have combined with controversy in the boardroom and stifling levels of debt have led to the current situation.

"We've always been first-class and last season was the first time in nearly 100 years that we'd ever been relegated," said Rolf Heller, president of the club known locally as "the moody diva on the river Main". But he says Eintracht Frankfurt will be back.

"We are at the bottom of the curve. I think we've stopped falling now and we should start going up from now on and I expect us to be back in the Bundesliga by our centenary year in 1999," Heller said.

Relegation is a costly business. Eintracht lost around around seven or eight million marks in revenues, another blow to the club's pride. Eintracht must also prove their financial solvency to keep their licence to play in the German league, which means stiff negotiations with their creditor banks.

The slide began with the sale of Eintracht's finest players two seasons ago, when Antony Yeboah and Maurizio Gaudino left under a cloud after a spate of disagreements with the then-coach Jupp Heynckes.

Ghanaian Yeboah, currently at Leeds United, was the Bundesliga's joint top scorer in 1992-93 and 1993-94 and has been sorely missed. Gaudino has since returned to Eintracht and is the fans' favourite.

"That was the beginning of the end. We had big plans -- European ambitions, winning the league. But as the success didn't come, we couldn't make the investments we planned. Problems developed which weren't addressed," said Heller.

Earlier in the season Eintracht president Hans-Joachim Otto and treasurer Bernd Thate resigned after tax authorities began investigating alleged tax irregularities at the club, relating to payments to Yeboah.
Heller was unwilling to comment on the issue but did say he thought Eintracht would emerge unscathed.
Mounting insecurity at boardroom level translated into trouble on the pitch. Eintracht sacked coach Dragoslav Stepanovic and manager Bernd Hoelzenbein left the club.

Local boy Rolf Heller reluctantly took over. A career administrator who has spent years working in the game at club and European level, Heller has long been associated with Eintracht and is untainted by recent controversies.

At the club's recent annual meeting, Eintracht treasurer Gaetano Patella said the club needed 4.5 million marks to get back into the top flight. But its finances are in better shape than previously thought, with debts of 6.8 million marks.
"We are looking at a number of possibilities to help us consolidate financially. Debt at a German football club is a different thing from at an Italian football club," said Heller.
"In Italy operating day-to-day with negative equity is not so much an issue. But here in Germany you can have terrible difficulties getting credit from banks, for example."

Heller has spoken to a number of investors and is examining a number of options to change the group's structure but there is no immediate prospect of the club going public and becoming Eintracht Frankfurt AG, or Plc, along the lines of many English clubs -- not for the time being anyway.
"Things will change with the clubs here in Germany and they will open up. These clubs were set up around a hundred years ago under completely different economic conditions.
"Bayern Munich is thinking about this option, Hamburg SV tried something, but I don't think Eintracht will become a quoted company, it wouldn't be realistic for the next few years."
"We've seen an average of 15,000 fans at home, even when the games were catastrophic and that's impressive. When we were top of the second division we had 28,000 fans coming along," said Heller.
It may be many years, if ever, before Frankfurt can think of reaching the dizzy heights they knew in the early 1960s. First, they have to climb out of the hole they currently find themselves in.
